body.head: The Last of the De Mullins: A Play Without a Preface
body.author: St. John Hankin
body.head:
THE LAST OF
THE DE MULLINS
A Play without a Preface
body.author: By St. John Hankin
body.subtitle: London: A. C. Fifield
body.p: Janet De Mullin....(Mrs. Seagrave) Hugo’s eldest daughter.

The action of the play takes place at Brendon Underwood in Dorset, Acts I and III at the Manor House, the De Mullins’ house in the village, Act II on the borders of Brendon Forest. Three days pass between Acts I and II, five between Acts II and III.

div.head: The Last of the De Mullins: A Play Without a Preface

div.p: Scene: The Inner Hall at the Manor House in Brendon-Underwood village. An old-fashioned white-panelled room. At the back is a big stone-mullioned Tudor window looking out on to the garden. On the left of this is a bay in which is a smaller window. A door in the bay leads out into the garden. People entering by this door pass the window before they appear. The furniture is oak, mostly Jacobean or older. The right-hand wall of the room is mainly occupied by a great Tudor fireplace, over which the De Mullin Coat of Arms is carved in stone. Above this a door leads to the outer hall and front door. A door on the opposite side of the room leads to the staircase and the rest of the house. The walls are hung with a long succession of family portraits of all periods and in all stages of dinginess as to both canvas and frame. When the curtain rises the stage is empty. Then Hester is seen to pass the window at the back, followed by Mr. Brown. A moment later they enter. Mr. Brown is a stout, rather unwholesome-looking curate, Hester a lean, angular girl of twenty-eight, very plainly and unattractively dressed in sombre tight-fitting clothes. She has a cape over her shoulders and a black hat on. Brown wears seedy clerical garments, huge boots and a squashy hat. The time is twelve o’clock in the morning of a fine day in September.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Come in, Mr. Brown. I’ll tell mother you’re here. I expect she’s upstairs with father (going towards door).

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Don’t disturb Mrs. De Mullin, please. I didn’t mean to come in.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: You’ll sit down now you are here?

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Thank you (does so awkwardly). I’m so glad to hear Mr. De Mullin is better. The Vicar will be glad too.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. Dr. Rolt thinks he will do all right now.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: You must have been very anxious when he was first taken ill.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: We were terribly anxious. [Hester takes off her hat and cape and puts them down on the window seat.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: I suppose there’s no doubt it was some sort of stroke?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Dr. Rolt says no doubt.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: How did it happen?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: We don’t know. He had just gone out of the room when we heard a fall. Mother ran out into the hall and found him lying by the door quite unconscious. She was dreadfully frightened. So were we all.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Had he been complaining of feeling unwell?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Not specially. He complained of the heat a little. And he had a headache. But father’s not strong, you know. None of the De Mullins are, Aunt Harriet says.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Mrs. Clouston is with you now, isn’t she?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. For a month. She generally stays with us for a month in the summer.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: I suppose she’s very fond of Brendon?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: All the De Mullins are fond of Brendon, Mr. Brown.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Naturally. You have been here so long.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Since the time of King Stephen.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Not in this house?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: (smiling)
Not in this house, of course. It’s not old enough for that.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Still, it must be very old. The oldest house in the Village, isn’t it?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Only about four hundred years. The date is 1603. The mill is older, of course.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: You still own the mill, don’t you?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. Father would never part with it. He thinks everything of the mill. We get our name from it, you know. De Mullin. Du Moulin. “Of the Mill.”

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Were the original De Mullins millers then?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: (rather shocked at such a suggestion)
Oh no!

div.head: BROWN
div.p: I thought they couldn’t have been. .

div.head: HESTER
div.p: No De Mullin has ever been in trade of any kind! But in the old days to own a mill was a feudal privilege. Only lords of manors and the great abbeys had them. The farmers had to bring all their corn to them to be ground.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: I see.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: There were constant disputes about it all through the Middle Ages.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Why was that?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: The farmers would rather have ground their corn for themselves, I suppose.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Why? If the De Mullins were willing to do it for them?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: They had to pay for having it ground, of course.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: (venturing on a small joke)
Then the De Mullins were millers, after all, in a sense.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: You mustn’t let father hear you say so!

div.head: BROWN
div.p: The mill is never used now, is it?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: No. When, people gave up growing corn round here and all the land was turned into pasture it fell into decay, and now it’s almost ruinous.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: What a pity!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. Father says England has never been the same since the repeal of the Corn laws. (Enter Mrs. De Mullin and Mrs. Clouston by the door on the left, followed by Dr. Rolt.) Here is mother—and Aunt Harriet.

p.hi: Mrs. De Mullin, poor lady, is a crushed, timid creature of fifty-eight or so, entirely dominated by the De Mullin fetish and quite unable to hold her own against either her husband or her sister-in-law, a hardmouthed, resolute woman of sixty. Even Hester she finds almost too much for her. For the rest a gentle, kindly lady, rather charming in her extreme helplessness. Rolt is the average country doctor, brisk, sensible, neither a fool nor a genius.

div.head: ROLT
div.p: (as they enter the room)
He’s better. Distinctly better. A little weak and depressed, of course. That’s only to be expected. Good morning.
[Shakes hands with Hester. Nods to Brown.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Mr. De Mullin is always nervous about himself.

div.head: ROLT
div.p: Yes. Constitutional, no doubt. But he’ll pick up in a few days. Keep him as quiet as you can. That’s really all he needs now.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You don’t think he ought to stay in his room?
... Good morning, Mr. Brown. Are you waiting to see me?
[Brown shakes hands with both ladies.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: (awkwardly)
Not specially. I walked over from the church with Miss De Mullin.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Is father coming downstairs, mother?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes, Hester. He insisted on getting up. You know he always hates staying in his room.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Oh, Dr. Rolt, do you think he should?

div.head: ROLT
div.p: I don’t think it will do him any harm. He can rest quietly in a chair or on the sofa.... Well, I must be off. Good-bye, Mrs. De Mullin.
[Shakes hands briskly with every one.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: (rising ponderously)

I must be going too (shakes hands with Mrs. De Mullin). You’ll tell Mr. De Mullin I inquired after him? Good-bye, Mrs. Clouston (shakes hands). And you’re coming to help with the Harvest Decorations on Saturday, aren’t you, Miss De Mullin?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Of course.
[Brown and Rolt go out.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON

p.hi: (seating herself and beginning to knit resolutely)

div.p: What singularly unattractive curates the Vicar seems to get hold of, Jane!.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Do you think so, Harriet?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Quite remarkably. This Mr. Brown, for instance. He has the most enormous feet! And his boots! I’ve never seen such boots!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: We needn’t sneer if Mr. Brown doesn’t wear fine clothes, Aunt Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Of course not Hester. Still, I think he goes to the opposite extreme. And he really is quite abnormally plain. Then there was that Mr. Snood, who was curate when I was down last year. The man with the very red hands. (These acid comments are too much for Hester, who flounces out angrily. Mrs. Clouston looks up for a moment, wondering what is the meaning of this sudden disappearance. Then continues unmoved.) I’m afraid the clergy aren’t what they were in our young days, Jane.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I don’t think I’ve noticed any falling off.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: It is there all the same. I’m sure Hugo would agree with me. Of course, curates are paid next to nothing. Still, I think the Vicar might be more happy in his choice.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I believe the poor like him.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON

p.hi: (to whom this seems of small importance compared with his shocking social disabilities)

div.p: Very likely.... Do please keep still, Jane, and don’t fidget with that book. What is the matter with you?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m a little nervous this morning. Hugo’s illness...

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Hugo’s almost well now.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Still the anxiety...

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Nonsense, Jane. Anxiety is not at all a thing to give way to, especially when there’s no longer anything to be anxious about. Hugo’s practically well now. Dr. Rolt seems to have frightened us all quite unnecessarily.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I suppose it’s difficult to tell.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Of course, it’s difficult. Otherwise no one would send for a doctor. What are doctors for if they can’t tell when a case is serious and when it is not?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: But if he didn’t know?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Then he ought to have known. Next time Hugo is ill you’d better send to Bridport. (Mrs. De Mullin drops book on table with a clatter) Really, Jane, what are you doing? Throwing books about like that!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: It slipped out of my hand.,,
[Rises and goes up to window restlessly.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Is anything wrong?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, the truth is I’ve done something, Harriet, and now I’m not sure whether I ought to have done it. Mrs. Clouston
Done what?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m afraid you won’t approve.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Perhaps you’d better tell me what it is. Then we shall know.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: The fact is some one is coming here this morning, Harriet—to see Hugo.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: To see Hugo? Who is it?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Janet?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Janet! She wouldn’t dare!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I sent for her, Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You sent for her?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. When Hugo was first taken ill and Dr. Rolt seemed to think the attack was so serious....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Dr. Rolt was a fool.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Very likely, Harriet. But he said Hugo might die. And he said if there was any one Hugo would wish to see....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: But would Hugo wish to see Janet?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I thought he might. After all Janet is his daughter. Mrs. Clouston
I thought he said he would never see her again?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He did say that, of course. But that was eight years ago. And, of course, he wasn’t ill then.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: When did you send for her?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Three days ago.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Why didn’t she come then, if she was coming at all?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She was away from home. That was so unfortunate. If she had come when Hugo was ill in bed it might have been all right. But now that he’s almost well again....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: When did you hear she was coming?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Only this morning. Here is what she says..
[Produces telegram from pocket.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: “Telegram delayed. Arrive mid-day. Seagrave.” Seagrave?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. She calls herself Mrs. Seagrave now.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: On account of the child, I suppose.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I suppose so.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I never could understand how Janet came to go so wrong. (Mrs. De Mullin sighs.) None of the De Mullins have ever done such a thing before.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m sure she doesn’t get it from my family.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Well, she must have got it from somewhere. She’s not in the least like a De Mullin.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: (lamentably)
I believe it was all through bicycling.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Bicycling?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. When girls usen’t to scour about the country as they do now these things didn’t happen.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I never approved of Janet’s bicycling you remember, Jane.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Nor did I, Harriet. But it was no use. Janet only laughed. Janet never would do what she was told about things even when she was quite a child. She was so very obstinate. She was always getting some idea or other into her head. And when she did nothing would prevent her from carrying it out. At one time she wanted to teach.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I remember.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She said girls ought to go out and earn their own living like boys.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: What nonsense!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: So Hugo said. But Janet wouldn’t listen. Finally we had to let her go over and teach the Aldenham girls French three times a week, just to keep her amused.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: It was strange you never could find out who the father was.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. She wouldn’t tell us.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You should have made her tell you. Hugo should have insisted on it.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hugo did insist. He was terribly angry with her. He sent her to her room and said she was not to come down till she told us. But it was no use. Janet just stayed in her room till we had all gone to bed and then took the train to London.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You should have locked her door.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: We did. She got out of the window.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Got out of the window! The girl might have been killed.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. But Janet was always fond of climbing. And she was never afraid of anything.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: But there’s no late train to London.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She caught the mail at Weymouth, I suppose.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Do you mean to say she walked all the way to Weymouth in the middle of the night? Why, it’s twelve miles.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She had her bicycle as I said.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Tck!... How did you know she went to London?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She wrote from there, for her things.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I wonder she wasn’t ashamed.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: So Hugo said. However, he said I might send them. But he made me send a letter with the things to say that he would have nothing more to do with her and that she was not to write again. For a time she didn’t write. Nearly five months. Then, when her baby was born, she wrote to tell me. That was how I knew she had taken the name of Seagrave. She mentioned it.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Did you show the letter to Hugo?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: What did he say?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Nothing. He just read it and gave it back to me without a word.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: That’s the last you’ve heard of her, I suppose?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Oh no, Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Do you mean to say she goes on writing? And you allow her? When Hugo said she was not to?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. Not often, Harriet. Only occasionally.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: She has no business to write at all.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Her letters are quite short. Sometimes I wish they were longer. They really tell one nothing about herself, though I often ask her.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You ask her! Then you write too!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I answer her letters, of course. Otherwise she wouldn’t go on writing. ‘

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Really, Jane, I’m surprised at you. So you’ve actually been corresponding with Janet all these years—and never told me! I think you’ve behaved very badly.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I didn’t like to, Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Didn’t like to!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: And as you don’t think I ought to hear from her....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON.
div.p: I don’t think you ought to hear from her, of course. But as you do hear naturally I should like to have seen the letters.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I didn’t know that, Harriet. In fact, I thought you would rather not. When a dreadful thing like this happens in a family it seems best not to write about it or to speak of it either, doesn’t it? Hugo and I never speak of it.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Does Hugo know you hear from her?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I think not. I have never told him. Nor Hester. I’m sure Hester would disapprove.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: My dear Jane, what can it matter whether Hester approves or not? Hester knows nothing about such things. At her age!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hester is twenty-eight.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Exactly. A girl like that.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Girls have such very strong opinions nowadays. Mrs. Clouston
What does Janet live on? Teaching?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I suppose so. She had her Aunt Miriam’s legacy, of four hundred pounds of course.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Only four hundred pounds.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I never approved of that legacy, Jane. Girls oughtn’t to have money left them. It makes them too independent.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Aunt Miriam was always so fond of Janet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Then she should have left the money to Hugo. Fathers are the proper people to leave money to.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hugo did have the management of the money—till Janet was twenty-one.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Why only till she was twenty-one?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: It was so in Aunt Miriam’s will. Of course, Hugo would have gone on managing it for her. It was very little trouble as it was all in Consols. But Janet said she would rather look after it for herself.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Ridiculous! As if girls could possibly manage money!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: So Hugo said. But Janet insisted. So she got her way.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: What did she do with it? Spend it?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No. Put it into a Railway, she said.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: A Railway! How dangerous!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She said she would prefer it. She said Railways sometimes went up. Consols never.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: She lost it all, of course?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I don’t know, Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You don’t know?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No. I never liked to ask. Hugo was rather hurt about the whole thing, so the subject was never referred to.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Let me see. The child must be eight years old by now.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Just eight. It will be nine years next March since Janet went away.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: What did she call him?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Johnny.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Johnny! None of the De Mullins have ever been called Johnny.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Perhaps it was his father’s name.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Perhaps so (pause).

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Do you think I ought to tell Hugo about Janet’s coming?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Certainly.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I thought perhaps....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Nonsense, Jane. Of course, he must be told. You ought to have told him from the very beginning?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Do you mean when I sent the telegram? But Hugo was unconscious.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: As soon as he recovered consciousness then.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I did mean to. But he seemed so weak, and Dr. Rolt said any excitement....

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Dr. Rolt!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, I couldn’t tell that Dr. Rolt knew so little about Hugo’s illness, could I? And I was afraid of the shock.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Still, he should have been told at once. It was the only chance.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. I see that now. But I was afraid of the shock, as I said. So I put it off. And then, when I didn’t hear from Janet, I thought I would wait.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Why?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You see I didn’t know whether she was coming. And if she didn’t come, of course there was no necessity for telling Hugo anything about it. I’m afraid he’ll be very angry.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: At any rate, you must tell him now. The sooner the better.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Very well, Harriet. If you think so.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You had better go up to him at once.
[Mrs. De Mullin goes to the door on the left, opens it, then draws back hastily.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Here is Hugo. He’s just coming across the hall. With Hester. How unlucky.
MRS. CLOUSTON I don’t see that it matters.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’d rather not have told him before Hester.

[Mrs. Clouston shrugs her shoulders. A moment later Hugo enters. He leans on a stick and Hester’s arm. He looks weak and pale and altogether extremely sorry for himself, obviously a nervous and a very tiresome patient.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Carefully, father. That’s right. Will you lie on the sofa?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: No. Put me in the armchair. I’m tired of lying down.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Very well. Let me help you. There. Wait a moment. I’ll fetch you some pillows.

p.hi: [Props him up on pillows in an armchair.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Thank you.

p.hi: [Lies back exhausted and closes his eyes.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: How are you feeling now, Hugo?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Very weak.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I wonder if you ought to have come down?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: It won’t make any difference. Nothing will make any difference any more, Jane. I shan’t last much longer. I’m worn out.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Father!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes, Hester. Worn out (with a sort of melancholy pride). None of the De Mullins have been strong. I’m the last of them. The last of the De Mullins.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Come, Hugo, you mustn’t talk in that morbid way.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m not morbid, Harriet. But I feel tired, tired.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You’ll be better in a day or two.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: No, Jane. I shall never be better. Never in this world (pause).

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hugo... there’s something... something I have to tell you....

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: What is it, Jane? (fretfully). What have you been keeping from me?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I ought to have told you before. Only I didn’t like...

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Is it something about my illness?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Oh no, Hugo.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I thought Dr. Rolt might have said something.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: It’s nothing of that kind.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, well, what is it?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hugo, some one is coming here to-day, to see you.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: To see me? Who?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You won’t be angry, Hugo?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: How can I possibly say that, Jane, when I don’t know who it is?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hugo, it’s... (Bell rings loudly.) Harriet, there’s the bell! I wonder if it’s she? Do you think it is?
[All look towards the door on the right, expectantly.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, Jane? Am I to hear who this visitor is or am I not?

p.hi: (showing in a lady leading a little boy by the hand)

div.head: MRS. SEAGRAVE
div.p: [Enter Janet and Johnny!. Janet is a very handsome woman of six-and-thirty. She is admirably dressed, but her clothes are quiet and in excellent taste, dark in colour and plain in cut but expensive. Her hat is particularly tasteful, but also quiet. Her clothes are in marked contrast to those of her mother and sister which are of the homeliest description and were probably made in the village. Johnny is a well-grown youngster of eight in a sailor suit.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Mother!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, my dear! (cry of welcome).

div.head: JANET
div.p: Father! (Drops Johnny’s hand, comes rapidly to him, falls on one knee and kisses him impulsively, patting his left hand with her right.) How are you? Better? (holding out her left hand to her mother but still kneeling). How do you do, mother dear? (Mrs. De Mullin takes it. Puts her other hand on Janet’s shoulder.) I should have come before, father, directly you sent for me. But your telegram was delayed. I was away from home.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I see.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Have you been very ill, father? And did you frighten them all dreadfully? How naughty of you!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Silly Janet! Let me look at you, my dear. (Looks at her face as she holds it up.) You’re not much changed, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nor are you, father.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: A little greyer, perhaps.

div.head: JANET
div.p: No! Not a hair!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, my dear, Pm glad you’ve come. We parted in anger, but that’s all over now. Forgotten and forgiven. Eh?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. Forgotten and forgiven (rises). How are you, Aunt Harriet? I didn’t see you. (Eagerly) Hester!

p.hi: [Goes to her impulsively, holding out her hand. Hester takes it coldly. Janet tries to draw her towards her. Hester resists. She drops her hand and Hester turns away.]

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Who is that? (pointing to Johnny).

div.head: JANET
div.p: (turning to him)
That is Johnny. My son.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: My grandson?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. I had to bring him, father. We were away from home and there was no one to leave him with.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m glad you brought him. Come here, Johnny. Don’t be afraid.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: I’m not afraid. Why should I be afraid?
[Goes to him.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Say “How do you do, grandfather.”

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: How do you do, grandfather?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Will you give me a kiss, Johnny?

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: If you like, grandfather.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: That’s a good boy.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Kiss your grandmother too, Johnny.

p.hi: [Mrs. De Mullin snatches him up and kisses him passionately. Then holds him a little way off and looks at him admiringly.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: What a fine little fellow, Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Isn’t he, mother? And so strong and healthy! He’s hardly had a day’s illness since he was born.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: (who has been staring at the pictures on the walls, holding his grandmother by one hand).
Who are all these old men, grandfather?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Your ancestors, my boy.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: What’s ancestors?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Your forefathers. Your mother’s forefathers,

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Is that old man in the wig an ancestor?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. That is Anthony De Mullin, your great-great-grandfather.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: What was he?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: (puzzled)
What was he? I don’t know that he was anything in particular. He was just a gentleman.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Is that all?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Don’t make any mistake, my boy. It’s a great thing to be descended from gentle-people, a thing to be proud of and to be thankful for.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Mother says the great thing is for every one to be of some use in the world. Are gentle-people of more use in the world than other people, grandfather?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Certainly.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: And were all these old men gentle-people?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: All of them. And you must grow up like them.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: They’re very ugly, grandfather (pause). What did they do?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: They lived down here at Brendon.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Nothing else?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: They looked after their land.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Had they much land?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: A great deal. At one time the De Mullins owned all the land about here.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: How much do they own now?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Not very much, I’m afraid.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Then they can’t have looked after it very well, can they, grandfather?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Now, Hugo, do you think you ought to talk any more? Why not go upstairs for a little and lie down?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Perhaps I will, Jane. I am a little tired.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Shall I go with father?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No. I will. Come, Hugo (helps him up).

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Will you come, with me, Johnny?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No, Hugo. He will only disturb you. Stay down here, Johnny, with your mother. Now then. Carefully.

p.hi: [Leads De Mullin off by the door on the left. There is a pause, during which the remaining occupants of the room obviously have nothing in particular to say to each other. At last Mrs. Clouston speaks.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Well, Janet, how have you been all these years?

div.head: JANET
div.p: All right, Aunt Harriet. And you?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Pretty well, thanks.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Are you still living down at Bath?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Yes. You live in London, Jane tells me.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: What do you do there? Teach?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh no. Why should I be teaching?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Jane said you wanted to teach at one time.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That was years ago. Before I left Brendon. soon gave up that idea. No. I keep a shop.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: A shop!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. A hat-shop

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Good heavens! A De Mullin in a hat-shop!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not a De Mullin, Aunt Harriet. A Seagrave.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Did Mr. Seagrave keep a hat-shop?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Seagrave?... oh, I see. No. It’s not a man’s hat shop. It’s a lady’s (takes off hat). This is one of ours. What do you think of it, Hester?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: It looks very expensive.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, I own I’m rather pleased with it.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You seem to be able to dress very well altogether, in spite of the shop.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Because of it, Aunt Harriet. That’s the advantage of being what is called “in trade.” If I were a school teacher or a governess or something genteel of that kind I could only afford to dress like a pauper. But as I keep a shop I can dress like a lady. Clothes are a question of money, after all, aren’t they?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: If one is in a shop it doesn’t matter how one dresses.

div.head: JANET
div.p: On the contrary if one is in a shop it matters a great deal. A girl in a shop must dress well. The business demands it. If you ever start a hat-shop, Aunt Harriet, you’ll have to dress very differently. Otherwise nobody will buy your hats.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Indeed? Fortunately I’ve no intention of starting a shop of any kind.

div.head: JANET
div.p: No! Well, I expect you’re wise. I doubt if you’d make a success of it.
[Loud ring heard off.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I hope that’s not a visitor. (Janet stares Then laughs good-humouredly. Aunt Harriet’s nervous desire to keep her out of the way of visitors strikes her as amusing.) What are you laughing at, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nothing, Aunt Harriet.

div.head: ELLEN
div.p: Miss Deanes. Mr. Brown.
[Miss Deanes is a bulky, red-faced, shortsighted woman of forty-two, very fussy and absurd in manner, who talks very fast. Brown carries a book.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: How do you do, Mrs. Clouston. Such a piece of news! I felt I must tell you. I brought Mr. Brown with me. He was just leaving a book for you, Hester, so I made him come in.
[Shakes hands with Hester.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Here it is, Miss De Mullin. It’s the one you wanted to borrow. Blore on the Creeds.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Thank you.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Janet! Is that you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Miss Deanes. How are you?
[Shakes hands.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Good gracious, child, when did you come? Why, you’ve not been down to Brendon for years.

div.head: JANET
div.p: It is a long time, isn’t it?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: And who is this young gentleman?
[Noticing Johnny who is holding Janet’s hand and staring at Miss Deanes.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That is my son. Shake hands with Miss Deanes, Johnny.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Your son! There now! And I never knew you were even married!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Didn’t you!

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: No.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I forgot. I haven’t introduced you. Mr. Brown—Mrs. Seagrave.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: How do you do.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: And now what is your piece of news, Miss Deanes?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Oh yes. I must tell you. You’d never guess. Somebody else is engaged to be married, (to Janet) Who do you think?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’ve no idea.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Bertha Aldenham—to Mr. Bulstead.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Bulstead?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Yes. But I forgot. You wouldn’t know them. They didn’t come here till long after you went away. They bought Brendon Park from the Malcolms three years ago. You remember the Malcolms, Janet? Janet (whose attention has wandered)
Eh? Oh yes, of course.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Which Mr. Bulstead is it? The eldest?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Yes. Montague.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Monty Bulstead! Engaged!

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Are the Aldenhams pleased?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Very, I expect. The Bulsteads are so rich, you see.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Does he live down here; this Mr. Montagu Bulstead, I mean?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Oh no. He’s here on leave. He’s in the army. He only got back three months ago (with a little giggle). He and Bertha haven’t taken long to settle things, have they?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, they haven’t taken long.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: But I dare say he will live here when he’s married. As the Bulsteads are so rich.- The father makes frilling and lace and so on. All those things people used to make so much better by hand. And Bertha may not care about army life. I know I shouldn’t. (Janet smiles discreetly.) It’s not always very nice, is it?

div.head: BROWN
div.p: (to Johnny who has been staring at him roundeyed across the room, with heavy geniality).
Well, young man. Who are you staring at, eh? Do you want to talk to me?

div.head: JOHNNY

p.hi: (quite simply, in his high piping treble)

div.p: No, thank you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Sh! Johnny! You don’t mean that. Go to Mr. Brown when he speaks to you.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Very well, Mummie.
[Does so slowly.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Now then what shall we talk about, you and I?

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: I don’t know.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Don’t you? Suppose we see if you can say your catechism then? Would you like that?

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: What’s catechism?

div.head: BROWN
div.p: Come, Johnny, I’m sure your mother has taught you your catechism.. Can you repeat your “Duty towards your Neighbour”? (Johnny shakes his head emphatically). Try “My duty towards my neighbour....

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Mother says it’s every one’s duty to be healthy and to be happy! Is that what you mean?

div.head: BROWN
div.p: No! No!

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Well, that’s what mother taught me.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’m afraid he doesn’t know his catechism yet, Mr. Brown. You see he’s only eight. (Brown bows stiffly.) Run away, Johnny, and play in the garden for a little.

p.hi: [Leads him to the door in the bay.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: All right, Mummie.
[Johnny runs out into the garden. A certain relief is perceptible on his departure. It is felt that his interview with Mr. Brown has not been a success....

div.head: MISS DEANES

p.hi: (who feels that a change of subject will be only tactful)

div.p: There now, Hester! I do believe you’ve never asked after Dicky! He’ll be so offended!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Has Dicky been ill again? I thought you said he was better yesterday.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: He was. But he had a relapse, poor darling. I had to sit up all last night with him!

div.head: JANET
div.p: What has been the matter with him?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Some sort of chill, Dr. Rolt said. I was dreadfully anxious.

div.head: JANET
div.p: What a pity! ‘Colds are such troublesome things for children.

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: (puzzled)
Children?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. You were speaking of a child, weren’t you? Miss Deanes
Oh no. Dicky is my cockatoo. He’s the sweetest bird. Talks quite like a human being. And never a coarse expression. That’s so unusual with cockatoos.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Indeed?

div.head: MISS DEANES
div.p: Yes. The voyage, you see. They come all the way from South America and generally they pick up the most dreadful language, poor lambs—from the sailors.
But Dicky didn’t. He has such a pure mind (rising). And now I really must be going. I have all kinds of people I want to tell about Mr. Bulstead’s engagement.

p.hi: [Shaking hands with Mrs. Clouston and Janet.

div.head: BROWN
div.p: I must be off too. Wait one moment, Miss Deanes. Good-bye, Mrs. Clouston.

p.hi: [Shakes hands with Mrs. Clouston and bows stiffly to Janet. He has not yet forgiven Johnny for not knowing his catechism.

div.p: Good-bye, Miss De Mullin. Shall I see you at Evensong?
I expect so.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Poof!

div.head: JANET
div.p: What a fool Miss Deanes is!

div.head: MRS CLOUSTON
div.p: She always was, wasn’t she?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I suppose so. Going on in that way about her ridiculous cockatoo! And that hideous little curate!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I don’t see why you should sneer at all my friends.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Are they your friends, Hester? Then I won’t sneer at them. But you can’t call Mr. Brown handsome, can you?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Mr. Brown is a very good man and works very hard among the poor. That’s better than being handsome.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. But less agreeable, isn’t it? However, if you like him there’s an end of it. But he needn’t have begun asking Johnny his catechism the very first time he met him. I don’t call it good manners,

div.head: HESTER
div.p: How was he to know the poor child was being brought up to be a little heathen?

p.hi: [Takes up her hat and cape and begins putting them on.

div.head: JANET
div.p: How, indeed!

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Are you going out, Hester? Lunch will be ready in half an hour. .

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Only to take Mrs. Wason her soup, Aunt Harriet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Do you want to marry Mr. Brown, Hester?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: My dear Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, Aunt Harriet, there’s nothing to be ashamed of if she does. Do you, Hester?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Why do you ask such a question?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Never mind. Only answer it (pause). You do like him, don’t you?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I’ve a great respect for Mr. Brown.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Don’t blush, my dear. I dare say that’s much the same thing.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I won’t talk to you about it. You only sneer. Janet
I wasn’t sneering. Come, Hester, don’t be cross. Why shouldn’t we be friends? I might help you.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: How could you help me?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I might make you a hat, my dear.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Mr. Brown doesn’t notice those things.

div.head: JANET
div.p: All men notice those things, Hester.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I suppose that’s why you wear such fine clothes.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That’s it. Fine feathers make fine birds.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Well, I call it shameless.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear Hester, you’re always being ashamed of things. You always were, I remember. What is there to be ashamed of in that? What on earth were women given pretty faces and pretty figures for if not to make men admire them and want to marry them?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Well, your plan hasn’t been very successful so far, anyhow!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nor has yours, Hester.

[Hester makes exclamation of impatience and seems about to reply angrily. Then thinks better of it and goes out without a word. Janet follows her retreat with her eyes and smiles half cynically, half compassionately. The Curtain falls.
Scene: On the edge of Brendon Forest.

Time: three days later. A road runs along the hack of the stage front which it is separated by a fence and high hedge. In this hut somewhat to the right is a stile and also a gate. Round the trunk of a large tree to the left is a rough wooden seat. The stage is empty when the curtain rises. Fhen enter Mrs. De Mullin, Janet and Johnny. They approach stile from the left and come through gate. There isan exit on the right of the stage through the Forest.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I don’t think I’ll come any farther, mother.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You won’t come up to the house?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, thanks (rather grimly). I don’t want to see Mrs. Bulstead. And I’m sure Mrs. Bulstead doesn’t want to see me.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I wish Hester could have come.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why couldn’t she?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She’s at the church putting up the decorations. It’s the Harvest Thanksgiving to-morrow.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Brown!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, I told you you weren’t to laugh at Hester about Mr. Brown. It’s not kind.

div.head: JANET
div.p: It’s all right mother. Hester’s not here.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Still, I don’t like it, dear. It’s not quite...

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not quite nice. I know, mother. Not the way really refined and ladylike young women talk. But I’m only quite a common person who sells hats. You can’t expect all these refinements from me!
[Mrs. De Mullin sighs.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Are you going to turn back?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not at once. I’ll wait for you here a little with Johnny in case they’re out. Why, they’ve put a seat here. [She sits on the side farthest from the road.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Usen’t there to be one?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. Nor a gate in my time. Only a stile.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Very likely, dear. I don’t remember. I don’t often come this way.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I often used to come along it in the old days.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I dare say. Well, I must be getting on to my call or I shall be late. You’re sure you won’t come?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Quite, mother. Good-bye.
[Mrs. De Mullin goes of through the forest.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Where’s grandmother going, Mummie?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Up to the big house.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: What big house?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Brendon Park.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Mayn’t I go up to the big house too?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, dear. You’re to stay with mother.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Who lives at the big house?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nobody you know, dear.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: That’s why I asked, Mummie.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, don’t ask any more, sonny. Mother’s rather tired. Run away and play, there’s a good boy.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Very well, Mummie.

p.hi: [Johnny disappears into the wood. Janet falls into a brown study. Presently a footstep is heard coming along the roady but she seems to notice nothing. Then a young man climbs over the stile. He starts as he sees her and draws back, then advances eagerly, holding out his hand.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet, is that you!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: JANET! Here!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Our stile, Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Our stile.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: The stile where you and I first met.

div.head: JANET

p.hi: (relapsing for a moment into something like sentiment)

div.p: Yes. I thought I must see it again—for the sake of old times.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: How long ago it all seems!

div.head: JANET
div.p: It is a longish time, you know.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I believe that was the happiest month of my life, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Was it, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes (pause). I say, when did you come down? You don’t live at home any longer, do you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. I only came down three days ago.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: By Jove it is good to see you again. Why, it’s eight years since we used to be together, you and I.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nearly nine.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes... You’re not coming to live down here again, are you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No; why?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I thought perhaps...

div.head: JANET
div.p: Would you dislike it very much if I did, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Of course not.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Confess. You did feel it would be rather awkward?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Well, of course...

div.head: JANET
div.p: However you can set your mind at rest. I’m not. [His relief at this intelligence enables him to realize the pleasure he is getting from seeing her again.)

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I say, Janet, how well you’re looking! I believe you’re handsomer than ever.

div.head: JANET
div.p: (smiling)
Am I?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You know you are.
[Pause. He looks at her admiringly. She turns away with a little smile.

div.head: JANET

p.hi: (feeling that they are getting on to dangerous ground)

div.p: Well, Monty. Where have you been these eight years?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Abroad with my regiment. We’ve been ordered all over the place. I’ve been home on leave, of course. But not for the last three years. Not since father bought the Park. I’ve never been at Brendon since ... (pause).

div.head: JANET
div.p: Since we were here? Don’t blush, Monty. (He nods shamefacedly.) How did he come to buy the place?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It was just a chance. He saw it advertised, came and looked at it and bought it. He’s no idea I was ever at Brendon before (rather bitter laugh). None of them have. I have to pretend not to know my way about.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It seems safer. (Janet nods.) Sometimes I almost forget to keep it up. I’m such a duffer about things. But I’ve managed hitherto. And now, of course, it’s all right as I’ve been here three months. I may be supposed to know the beastly place by this time.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Beastly? You’re not very polite.
[Monty laughs shamefacedly.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You got my note, didn’t you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: What note?... Oh, eight years ago, you mean? Yes.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I left it with the woman at the lodgings. As you were coming over that afternoon, I thought it safer than sending a message. And of course I daren’t telegraph. (Janet nods.) I was awfully sick at having to go away like that. All in a moment. Without even saying good-bye. But I had to.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course. Was your mother badly hurt?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No. Only stunned. That was such rot. If people get chucked out of a carriage they must expect to get stunned. But of course they couldn’t know. The telegram just said “Mother hurt. Carriage accident. Come at once.” It got to me at the lodgings a couple of hours before you were coming. I had just time to chuck my things into a bag and catch the train. I wanted to come back after the mater was all right again. But I couldn’t very well, could I?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why not?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Well, the regiment was to sail in less than three weeks and the mater would have thought it rather rough if I’d gone away again. I’d been away six weeks as it was.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh yes. Of course.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: To think if I hadn’t happened to be riding along that road and seen you at the stile and asked my way, you and I might never have met. What a chance life is!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Just a chance (pause).

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Why did you go away, Janet? You weren’t going the last time I saw you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Wasn’t I?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No. At least you said nothing about it.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I didn’t know I was going then. Not for certain.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Why did you go?

div.head: JANET
div.p: (quietly) I had to, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You had to? (Janet nods.)But why?
Mother found out.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: About us?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. And she told father.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: (genuinely distressed) Oh, Janet! I’m so sorry.

div.head: JANET
div.p: It couldn’t be helped,

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Does he know who it was?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Who you were? No.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You didn’t tell him?

div.head: JANET
div.p: MONTY! As if I should.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I don’t know. Girls generally do.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I didn’t.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No. I suppose you wouldn’t. But you’re different from most girls. Do you know there was always something rather splendid about you, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: (curtseys)
Thank you.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I wonder he didn’t make you tell.

div.head: JANET
div.p: He did try of course. That was why I ran away.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I see. Where did you go to?

div.head: JANET
div.p: London.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: To London? All alone? (Janet nods) Why did you do that? And why didn’t you let me know?

div.head: JANET
div.p: You were out of England by that time.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But why London?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I had to go somewhere. And it seemed better to go where I shouldn’t be known. Besides it’s easier to be lost sight of in a crowd.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But what did you do when you got there?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I got a place in a shop, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: A shop? You!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, a hat-shop, in Regent Street. My dear Monty, don’t gape like that. Hat-shops are perfectly respectable places. Almost too respectable to judge by the fuss two of them made about employing me.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, when I applied to them for work they naturally asked if I had ever worked in a hat-shop before. And when I said “No” they naturally asked why I wanted to begin. In the innocence of my heart I told them. Whereupon they at once refused to employ me—not in the politest terms.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Poor Janet. What beastly luck! Still...
[Hesitates.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I mean naturally they couldn’t be expected...
At least I don’t mean that exactly.
Only... [Stops.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear Monty, I quite understand what you mean. You needn’t trouble to be explicit. Naturally they couldn’t be expected to employ an abandoned person like me to trim hats. That was exactly their view.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But I thought you said you did get a place in a shop? Janet
Yes. But not at either of those shops. They were far too virtuous.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: How did you do it?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Told lies, Monty. I believe that’s how most women get employment.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Told lies?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. I invented a husband, recently deceased, bought several yards of crêpe and a wedding ring. This is the ring.
[Takes off glove.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh, Janet, how beastly for you!
[Janet shrugs.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Everything seems to be “Beastly” to you, Monty. Brendon and telling lies and lots of other things. Luckily I’m less superfine.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Didn’t they find out?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. That was why I decided to be a widow. It made inquiries more difficult.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I should have thought it made them easier.

div.head: JANET
div.p: On the contrary. You can’t cross-question a widow about a recent bereavement. If you do she cries. I always used to look tearful directly my husband’s name was even mentioned. So they gave up mentioning it. Women are so boring when they will cry.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: They might have inquired from other people.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why should they? Besides there was no one to inquire from. I called him Seagrave—and drowned him at sea. You can’t ask questions of the sharks.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh, Janet, how can you joke about it?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I couldn’t—then. I wanted work-too badly. But I can now—with your kind permission, I mean.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: And you’ve been at the shop ever since?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not that shop. I was only there about six months —till baby was born, in fact...

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet, there was a baby!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course there was a baby.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh, Janet! And you never wrote! Why didn’t you write?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I did think of it. But on the whole I thought I wouldn’t. It would have been no good.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No good?

div.head: JANET
div.p: You were in India.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I was in England.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not then.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You ought to have written at once—directly your mother found out.

div.head: JANET
div.p: One week after you sailed, Monty (defiantly). Besides why should I write?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Why? I could have married you, of course.

div.head: JANET
div.p: If I’d asked you, you mean? Thank you, my dear Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No, I don’t. Of course I should have married you. I must have married you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I wonder if you would.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Certainly I should. I should have been bound in honour.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I see. Then I’m glad I never wrote.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You’re glad? Now?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. I’ve done some foolish things in my life, Monty, but none quite so foolish as that. To marry a schoolboy, not because he loves you or wants to marry you but because he thinks he’s “bound in honour.” No, thank you.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I don’t mean that. You know I don’t, Janet. I loved you, of course. That goes without saying. I’d have married you like a shot before, only the Governor would have made such a fuss. The Governor was so awfully straitlaced about this sort of thing. When I was sent away from Eton he made the most ghastly fuss.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Were you sent away from Eton for “this sort of thing”?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes—at least I don’t mean that either. But it was about a girl there. He was frightfully wild. He threatened to cut me off if I ever did such a thing again. Such rot! As if no one had ever been sent away from school before!

div.head: JANET
div.p: I didn’t know you’d been sent away from Eton.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Didn’t you? I suppose I didn’t like to tell you-for fear of what you’d think (bitterly). I seem to have been afraid of everything in those days. .

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not everything, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh, you know what I mean. I was awfully afraid of the Governor, I remember. I suppose all boys are if their parents rag them too much. But I would have married you, Janet, if I’d known. I would honestly.

div.head: JANET
div.p: What is the pay of a British subaltern, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: The Governor would have had to stump up, of course.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Poor Mr. Bulstead! He’d have liked that, I suppose? And what about your poor unhappy colonel? And all the other little subalterns?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Still, you ought to have written.

div.head: JANET
div.p: You never wrote.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I couldn’t. You know that. You never would let me. That was why I couldn’t send that note to you to tell you I was going away. You said my letters would be noticed.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, I forgot that. That’s the result of having a father who is what is called old-fashioned.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: JANET
div.p: All letters to the Manor House are delivered locked in a bag. They always have been since the Flood, I believe, or at least since the invention of the postal service. And, of course, father won’t have it altered, So every morning there’s the ritual of unlocking this absurd bag. No one is allowed to do that but father—unless he is ill. Then mother has the privilege. And of course he. scrutinizes the outside of every letter and directly it’s opened asks who it’s from and what’s inside it. Your letters would have been noticed at once.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: How beastly!

div.head: JANET
div.p: The penalty of having nothing to do, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I know. What a mess the whole thing is!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Just so. No. There was no way out of it except the hat-shop.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It’s awfully rough on you, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Never mind. I dare say I wasn’t cut out for the wife of a subaltern, Monty; whereas I make excellent hats.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You’re still making the d———d things?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. Only at another shop. The Regent Street place had no room for me when I was well enough to go back to work. But the woman who kept it gave me a recommendation to a friend who was starting in Hanover Street. A most superior quarter for a hatshop, Monty. In fact the superior quarter. Claude et Cie was the name.
(Monty (rather shocked)
A French shop?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No more French than you are, Monty. It was kept by a Miss Hicks, one of the most thoroughly British people you can possibly imagine. But we called ourselves Claude et Cie in order to be able to charge people more for their hats. You can always charge fashionable women more for their clothes if you pretend to be French. It’s one of the imbecilities of commerce. So poor dear Miss Hicks became Madame Claude and none of our hats cost less than seven guineas.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Do people buy hats at such a price?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh yes. Everybody in Society bought them. Claude et Cie was quite the rage that Season. Nobody who was anybody went anywhere else.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: She must have made a great deal of money.

div.head: JANET
div.p: On the contrary. She made nothing at all and narrowly escaped bankruptcy.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But I don’t understand. If her hats were so dear and everybody bought them?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Everybody bought them but nobody paid for them. In the highest social circles I believe people never do pay for anything—certainly not for their clothes. At least, nobody paid Miss Hicks, and at the end of six months she was owed £1,200 and hadn’t a penny to pay her rent.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Why didn’t she make them pay.

div.head: JANET
div.p: She did dun them, of course, but they only ordered more hats to keep her quiet which didn’t help Miss Hicks much. And when she went on dunning them they said they should withdraw their custom. In fact, she was in a dilemma. If she let the bills run on she couldn’t pay her rent. And if she asked her customers to pay their bills they ceased to be customers.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: How beastly!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not again, Monty!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: What did she do?

div.head: JANET
div.p: She didn’t do anything. She was too depressed. She used to sit in the back room where the hats were trimmed and weep over the materials, regardless of expense. Finally things came to a crisis. The landlord threatened to distrain for his rent. But just as it looked as if it was all over with Claude et Cie a capitalist came to the rescue. I was the capitalist.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. I’d an old Aunt once who was fond of me and left me a legacy when I was seventeen. Four hundred pounds.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: That wouldn’t go very far.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Four hundred pounds goes a longish way towards setting up a shop. Besides, it was nearly five hundred by that time. My shares had gone up. Well, I and my five hundred pounds came to the rescue. I paid the rent and the most clamorous of the creditors, and Miss Hicks and I became partners.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But what was the good of that if the business was worth nothing?

div.head: JANET
div.p: It was worth several hundred pounds to any one, who had the pluck to sue half the British aristocracy. I sued them. It was tremendous fun. They were simply furious. They talked as if they’d never been sued before! As for Miss Hicks she wept more than ever and said I’d ruined the business.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Hadn’t you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: That business. Yes. But with the £1,200—or as much of it as we could recover—we started a new one. A cheap hat-shop. Relatively cheap that is-for Hanover Street. We charged two guineas a hat instead of seven, 100 per cent, profit instead of... You can work it out for yourself. But then our terms were strictly cash, so we made no bad debts. That was my idea.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But you said nobody ever paid for their hats.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not in the highest social circles. But we drew our customers from the middle classes who live in South Kensington and Bayswater, and are not too haughty to pay for a hat if they see a cheap one.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But wasn’t it a frightful risk?

div.head: JANET
div.p: It was a risk, of course. But everything in life is a risk, isn’t it? And it succeeded, as I felt sure it would. We’re quite a prosperous concern nowadays, and I go over to Paris four times a year to see the latest fashions. That, my dear Monty, is the history of Claude et Cie.
[Pause.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: And you’ve never married, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No.
MONTY {hesitates)
Is it because...?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Because?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Because you still care for me?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Monty, don’t be vain.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I didn’t mean it like that. Janet, don’t laugh. Of course, I’m glad if you don’t care any more. At least, I suppose I ought to be glad. It would have been dreadful if you had gone on caring all these years and I not known. But did you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, Monty, I didn’t. You may set your mind at rest.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You’re sure?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Quite. I had too many other things to think of.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Do you mean that beastly shop?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I meant my baby.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Our baby. Is it alive?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course. What do you mean, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I thought, as you didn’t say... (thoughtfully) Poor little beast! (Janet makes gesture of protest.) Well, it’s rough luck on the little beggar, isn’t it? What’s become of him, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: What’s become of him! My dear Monty, what should have become of him? He’s quite alive as I said and particularly thriving.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Do you mean he’s living with you!.. But, of course, I forgot, you’re supposed to be married.

div.head: JANET
div.p: A widow, Monty. An inconsolable widow!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Where is he? In London?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. As a matter of fact he’s probably not fifty yards away. Over there.
[Points towards the wood.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet! (nervously looking round).

div.head: JANET
div.p: Frightened, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Of course not (shamefacedly)

div.head: JANET
div.p: Just a little?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet, let me see him.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Would you like to?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Of course I should. He’s my baby as well as yours if it comes to that. Do call him, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: All right, (calls) Johnny! (pause) John... ny! (‘To Monty) You mustn’t tell him, you know.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Of course not.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Yes, Mummie.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Come here for a minute. Mother wants to speak to you.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Very well, Mummie. (Enters r.) Oh, Mummie, I’ve found such a lot of rabbits. You must come and see them. (Seeing Monty for the first time, stares at him.) Oh!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Come here, youngster. Come and let me look at you. (Johnny goes to him slowly. Monty, grasping both hands, draws him to him, looking at him long and keenly.) He’s like you, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Is he?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes. He has your eyes. So your name’s Johnny, young man?

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Well, Johnny, will you give me a kiss? (Monty leans forward. He does so.) That’s right.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: And now, Mummie, come and look at my rabbits.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not yet, dear. Mother’s busy just now.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: May I go back to them then?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Suppose I won’t let you go?

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: I’ll make you—and so will Mummie.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Plucky little chap. Off with you.
[Kisses him again, then releases his hands. Johnny trots off r. again. Monty follows him with his eyes. Pause.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, Monty, what do you think of him?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I think he’s splendid.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Isn’t he? And such a sturdy little boy. He weighed ten pounds before he was a month old.
I say, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You’ll let me kiss you once more, won’t you? For the last time?... (she hesitates). You don’t mind?

div.head: JANET
div.p: (heartily) .
Of course not, Monty. You’re not married yet, you know.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: JANET! My dear, dear Janet!
[Seizes her and kisses her fiercely.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That’s enough, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I’m afraid I behaved like an awful brute to you, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh no.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes, I did. I ought to have married you. I ought to marry you still. On account of the boy.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh well, you can’t do that now in any case, can you —as you’re engaged to Bertha Aldenham.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You’ve heard about that? Who told you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: A worthy lady called Miss Deanes.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I know. A regular sickener.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear Monty!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Sorry.

div.head: JANET
div.p: She brought the good news. The very day I arrived as it happened. We’ve hardly talked of anything else at the Manor House since—except father’s illness, of course.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Why?

div.head: JANET
div.p: What else is there to talk about—in Brendon?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: That’s true. Isn’t it... (stops himself, looks at watch. Whistles.) Whew! [Rises.

div.head: JANET
div.p: What is it, Monty?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I say, Janet, I wonder if you’d mind going now?
Why?

div.head: JANET
div.p: [She rises too.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Well, the fact is I’m expecting some one here directly. I...

div.head: JANET
div.p: Bertha?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes. I was to meet her here at the stile at six.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Our stile, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes,... You don’t mind, do you—about my asking you to go, I mean?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Not in the least.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: But you’re not going?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why should I go?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh, well, I thought——-

div.head: JANET
div.p: That it wouldn’t be quite suitable for us to meet?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I didn’t mean that, of course. But I thought you mightn’t like—I mean it might be painful...
[Sits again.

div.head: JANET
div.p: For me to see her? On the contrary, I’m dying to see her.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet, sometimes I think you’re not quite human.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear boy, I’m extremely human—and therefore curious (pause). What’s she like, Monty? Now, I mean. She promised to be pretty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: She is pretty, I suppose (pause). I wonder if Bertha and I will ever have a son like Johnny!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Let’s hope so, Monty. For Bertha’s sake.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Isn’t that some one coming? (pause, listens), I expect it’s she (rising hastily and advancing towards stile). Is that you, Bertha?

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Oh! There you are. Yes. Isn’t it hot? (entering by gate which he opens for her). Am I punctual? (with a cry) Janet! When did you come home?
[Goes to her eagerly.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Only three days ago.
[Bertha kisses her.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Only three days! And you’ve never been up to see us.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I know. But with father ill

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Of course. I understand. I was only joking. How is Mr. De Mullin?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Much better. Not well yet, of course. But he gets stronger every day.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I’m so glad. I say, Janet, do you remember when you used to teach us French?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I was awfully troublesome, I remember.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I expect you were an awful duffer at it too, Bertha.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: What cheek!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Wasn’t she, Ja—(pulls himself up) Miss De Mullin?
[Janet smiles nervously.
Oh, yes.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I didn’t know you’d met Janet, Monty? Why didn’t you tell us?
[Quite unsuspicious of anything wrong. Merely curious.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It was some time ago.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Not at Brendon? You’ve never been at Brendon before.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: No. It was at Weymouth. I was there getting over typhoid years ago.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I remember, you told me. Eight or nine years ago, wasn’t it?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes (looks at watch). I say, Bertha, we must be off if we’re not to be late.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Give me two minutes to rest. The weather’s simply stifling.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Rot! It’s quite cool.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Then you must have been sitting here a long time. I’ve been walking along a dusty road and I’m not going to start yet. Besides I want to know all about you two meeting. Were you staying at Weymouth, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh no. I just bicycled over. Mr. Bulstead ran into me.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I like that. She ran into me.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Anyhow my front wheel buckled and he had to help me to put it right.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: What gallantry!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It was. The beastly thing took about half an hour. By the time it was over we seemed to have known each other for a lifetime (looks at watch). Two minutes is up. Time to start, Bertha.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: It isn’t.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: It is. You’ll be late for dressing to a certainty if you don’t go.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I like that. I can dress as quickly as you if it comes to that.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Oh no. I can dress in ten minutes. I’ll give you a quarter of an hour’s start and be down in the drawing-room five minutes before you’re ready. Is it a bet?

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Done. In sixpences. (To Janet) I’m staying at the Park for a few days longer, Janet. Come up and see me, won’t you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’m afraid I can’t promise. On account of father.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Well, after I’ve gone home then. Mother will want to see you. And so will Helen. And now I suppose I really must go. Come along, Monty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Not I. I needn’t go for a quarter of an hour. You have a quarter of an hour’s start.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: All right. Good-bye, Janet (kisses her). You won’t forget about coming as soon as you can? I go back home on Thursday.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I won’t forget. Good-bye. [Bertha goes off through the wood. Janet watches her go and there is a pause.) Yes, she is pretty, Monty. Very pretty.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: You don’t mind?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Her being pretty? Of course not. It’s a justification.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: A justification?

div.head: JANET
div.p: For forgetting me

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Janet, I’ve never done that. You know I haven’t.

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, Monty. Not again. [Pause.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I say, I as nearly as possible called you Janet right out before Bertha.

div.head: JANET
div.p: So I saw. You did call me Miss De Mullin, by the way,—which wasn’t very clever of you.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Did I? What an ass I am! But I don’t suppose she noticed.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I dare say not. (A shrill cry comes from the wood on the right. Then silence. Janet starts up.) What was that?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I don’t know.

div.head: JANET
div.p: It sounded like a child. Where did it come from? Over here, didn’t it?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I think so.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I hope Johnny... I must go and see... (A moment later Johnny runs in, sobbing, followed by Mrs. De Mullin and Bertha.) Johnny! What is it, my sweetheart?
[Runs to him.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Oh, Mummie, Mummie, I was running after the rabbits and I tripped over some nettles and they stung me.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He put his foot in a hole, Janet. He fell just as I met Bertha (shakes hands with Monty). How do you do Mr. Bulstead.

div.head: JANET
div.p: There! There! my pet. Did it hurt very much? Mother shall kiss it and make it well.
JOHNNY (sobs)
Oh-h-h—- [Does so.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Is he your son?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. Don’t cry any more, dear. Brave boys don’t cry, you know.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: It h-hurts so.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I know. But crying won’t make it hurt less, will it? So you must dry your eyes. Come now.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: All right, Mummie.
[Stills sobs gradually.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: I’d no idea you were married, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Hadn’t you?

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: No. When was it?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Eight years ago. Nearly nine. To Mr. Seagrave.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Is he down here with you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. My husband died soon after our marriage.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Poor Janet. I’m so sorry (pause). And it was before your marriage that Monty met you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: How do you know?

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: He called you Miss De Mullin.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN

p.hi: (pricking up her ears suspiciously at this.)

div.p: I didn’t know you had met my daughter before, Mr. Bulstead.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Nor did I. They met down at Weymouth quite by chance eight or nine years ago.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Indeed?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Yes... I say, Bertha, excuse my interrupting you. but we really must be off now if we’re not to be late.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: You want to win that bet!

div.head: MONTY
div.p: The bet’s off. There’s no time to give you any start. I must come too or I shan’t be in time myself and the Governor will simply curse.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Is Mr. Bulstead very fierce if people are late for dinner?

div.head: MONTY
div.p: Simply beastly.

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: How very unpleasant! I wonder if I’m wise to marry into the family?
[Shaking hands merrily with Mrs. DeMullin and Janet. Then goes off r., laughing merrily.

div.head: MONTY
div.p: I wonder (shakes hands with Mrs. De Mullin and Janet). Will you give me a kiss, old chap?
[To Johnny.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: That’s three times.
[Monty nods.
[Monty follows Bertha off r. A long pause. Mrs. De Mullin looks fixedly at Janet. Janet looks at the ground.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Mr. Montague Bulstead seems unusually fond of children, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Does he, mother?
[She does not look up.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. Johnny is rather old to be kissed by strangers.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I supposed he kissed him because he was brave about being stung.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He seems to have kissed him before. Twice.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I dare say. I didn’t notice.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Johnny did, apparently.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, it doesn’t matter anyway, does it? (Looks up defiantly. Meets her mother’s eyes full on her) Why do you look at me like that, mother?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Send Johnny away for a little, Janet. I want to speak to you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’d rather not, mother. He might hurt himself again.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He will be quite safe. Run away, Johnny. But don’t go too far.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: All right, grandmother.
[Johnny trots off into the wood. Pause.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, why did you never tell us you had met Mr. Bulstead before?

div.head: JANET
div.p: When?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Any time during the last three days, when we were speaking of his engagement.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’d forgotten all about it, mother.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Indeed? And why didn’t you tell us eight years ago, when you met him at Weymouth, when you were still “Miss De Mullin”?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mother, don’t badger me like this. If you want to ask me anything ask it.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, Mr. Bulstead is Johnny’s father.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Bulstead? Absurd!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Then why did you pretend not to have met him? Why did you conceal the fact of your meeting him from us eight years ago? And why has he concealed the fact from Bertha and the Bulsteads?
[Pause.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Very well, mother, if you’re determined to know you must know. Yes, he’s Johnny’s father.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Oh, Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother, if you didn’t want to know you shouldn’t have asked. I told you not to worry me. (Mrs. De Mullin begins to cry. Remorsefully,)
There, there, mother! Don’t cry. I’m sorry I was cross to you. Don’t let’s talk any more about it.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No, Janet, we must talk about it. There’s no use trying to hide things any longer. You must tell me the truth.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Much better not, mother. It won’t give you any pleasure to hear.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Still, I’d rather know, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: As you please. What do you want me to tell you? Mrs. De Mullin
