Everything. How did you come to be at Weymouth? I don’t remember your staying at Weymouth eight years ago.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I wasn’t staying there. But Monty was.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Monty!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Bulstead. Oh, what does it matter now?
He’d had typhoid and was there to recruit. I’d ridden over on my bicycle...

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Bicycle! I always said it was all through bicycling.

div.head: JANET
div.p: He ran into me, or I ran into him. I was rather shaken, and he asked me to come in and rest. It happened close to the house where he was lodging.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You went in! To his lodgings! A man you had never met before!

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear mother, when you have been thrown off a bicycle, ordinary conventions cease to apply. Besides, as a matter of fact, we had met once before—the day before, in fact.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Where?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Here. By this very stile. Monty was riding past and he asked me the way to somewhere—Thoresby, I think. I was standing by the stile. Next day I happened to ride into Weymouth. We collided—and the rest you know.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Were those the only times you met him, Janet?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course not, mother. After the Weymouth collision we met constantly, nearly every day. We used to meet out riding and I had tea with him lots of times in his rooms.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: How long did this go on?

div.head: JANET
div.p: More than a month—till he left Weymouth, in fact. Now, mother, is that all you want to know? Because if so we’ll drop the subject.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Oh, Janet, what will your father say!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Father? He won’t know.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Won’t know? But I must tell him.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Good heavens, why?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: In order that Mr. Bulstead may marry you, of course. Your father will insist on his marrying you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: If father attempts to do that, mother, I shall deny the whole story. And Monty will back me up.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He would never be so wicked.

div.head: JANET
div.p: He would have to if I ask him. It’s the least he could do.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Johnny is there to prove it.

div.head: JANET
div.p: There’s nothing to prove that Monty is Johnny’s father. Nothing whatever.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: But, Janet, why won’t you marry him?

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear mother, because I don’t want to, of course.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You don’t want to?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Great heavens, no. Why should I? Monty Bulstead isn’t at all the sort of man I should care to marry.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Why not?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Frankly, mother, because he’s not interesting enough. Monty’s a very nice fellow and I like him very much, but I don’t want to pass the remainder of my life with him. If I’m to marry anybody—and I don’t think I shall—it will have to be a rather more remarkable person than Monty Bulstead.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yet you did love him, Janet. You must have loved him... then.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh yes. Then. But that was ages ago, before Johnny was born. After that I didn’t care for anybody any more except Johnny.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: But, Janet, you ought to marry him, for Johnny’s sake.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Too late, mother. That should have been eight years ago to be any use.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Better too late than not at all.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Better not at all than too late.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: He seduced you, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Did he? I was twenty-seven. He was twenty. If either of us was to blame, wasn’t it I?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, you’re trying to screen him.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Dearest mother, you talk like a sentimental novel.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: And he’s to be allowed to marry Bertha Aldenham, just as if this had never happened?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why not? It’s not her fault, is it? And girls find it difficult enough to get married nowadays, goodness knows.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Still, she ought to be told, Janet. I think she must be told.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear mother, if she knows everybody will know, and the scandal will make all the dead and gone De Mullins turn in their graves. As for father it would simply kill him out of hand.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Poor father.

div.head: JANET
div.p: So, on the whole, I don’t think we’ll tell any one. Come, mother, it’s time we started. (More kindly) Poor mother. Don’t fret. Perhaps Hester will have some news to cheer you when we get home.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hester?

div.head: JANET
div.p: An engagement, mother. Hester’s engagement. Hester and Mr. Brown have been decorating the church for the last four hours. What an opportunity for a declaration! Or don’t people propose in church?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, how can you laugh after what has happened?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Laugh? Of course I can laugh. What else is there to do? Let’s go home. Johnny! Johnny! (calls).
[By this time twilight is falling. A full moon has begun to risey lighting uf the scene.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Yes, Mummie.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Come along, dear. Mother’s going to start. Johnny (off r.)
All right, Mummie. (entering r.) Oh, Mummie, you’ve not seen my rabbits yet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. It’s too dark to-night. Mother must come and see them another time.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: You won’t forget, will you, Mummie? (looking at Mrs. De Mullin) Grandmother, you’ve been crying. Is that because I stung myself with a nettle?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Little egoist! Of course it is. Give your grandmother a kiss and we’ll all walk home together.
[Mrs. De Mullin stoop and kisses Johnny passionately. They go off through the gate and the curtain falls.
Five days have passed since Act II
Scene: As in Act I
Time: Late afternoon
[When the curtain rises Mrs. Clouston, Mrs. De Mullin, and Janet are on the stage. The nervous tension of the last few days has clearly told on Janet, who looks feverish and irritable.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: (speaking off into the hall on the right) Good-bye. Good-bye.

div.head: JANET
div.p: (who is standing about c., scornfully) Good-bye! Good-bye!

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: How many times a week does that Bulstead woman think it necessary to call on us?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: She doesn’t call very often.

div.head: JANET
div.p: She’s been three times this week.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Naturally she wants to hear how your father is, dear.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear mother, what can it matter to Mrs. Bulstead whether father lives or dies?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother, do you seriously believe she cares? Or Miss Deanes? Or Miss Rolt? Or any of these people? They only call because they’ve nothing better to do. It’s sheer mental vacuity on their part. Besides, father’s perfectly well now. They know that. But they go on calling, calling! I wonder Miss Deanes doesn’t bring her cockatoo to inquire.
[Tramps to and fro impatiently.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Really, Janet, I can’t think what’s the matter with you. Do sit down and try and exercise some selfcontrol.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’ve no self-control where these Brendon people are concerned. They get on my nerves, every one of them.... Where’s Johnny?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: In the garden, I think,

div.head: JANET
div.p: Sensible boy! He’s had enough of visitors for one day, I’ll be bound. I’ll go out and join him.
[Goes out angrily.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: I can’t think what’s come to Janet the last day or two. Her temper gets worse and worse.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Perhaps it’s only the hot weather. No De Mullin—-

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Nonsense, Jane, don’t be foolish. We can’t have Janet giving way to that sort of thing at her age.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m afraid she is rather irritable just now. She flew out quite savagely at Hester to-day just after luncheon.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Why was that?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Because of something she had been teaching Johnny. The Athanasian Creed I think it was. Yes, it must have been that because Johnny asked Janet what was meant by three Incomprehensibles. Janet asked him where he had heard all that and Johnny said Aunt Hester had taught it to him. Janet was very angry and forbade Hester ever to teach him anything again. Hester was quite hurt about it.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Naturally. Still, I do think Hester might have chosen something else to teach him.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: That was what Janet said.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: But that’s no reason why she shouldn’t behave herself when visitors are here. She was quite rude to Mrs. Bulstead. What they think of her in London when she goes on like this I can’t imagine.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Perhaps she isn’t like this in London.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Of course she is, Jane. Worse. Here she has the restraining influences of home life. Whereas in London, living alone as she does...

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She has Johnny.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: She has Johnny, of course. But that’s not enough. She ought to have a husband to look after her.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.
[Seats herself slowly beside her sister.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Where’s Hester?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: At church, I expect.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Church! Why the girl’s always at church.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: It’s a Wednesday. And it does no harm, I think.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Let us hope not, Jane.
[De Mullin enters by the door on the left. He has evidently got over his recent attack and looks comparatively hale and vigorous.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Have you had your nap, Hugo?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. The sunset woke me, I suppose. It was shining full on my face.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: What a pity it woke you.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: It didn’t matter. I’ve slept enough... (wanders towards sofa, c.). Where’s Johnny?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: In the garden, I think, with Janet.

div.head: DE MULLIN

p.hi: (wanders to window, c., and looks out)

div.p: Yes. There he is. He’s playing hide and seek with Ellen.... Now she’s caught him. No, he’s got away. Bravo, Johnny! (Stands watching intently for a while. Then turns and comes down c.) What a fine little fellow it is! A true De Mullin!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Do you think so, Hugo?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Every inch of him! (pause, sits c., half to himself) If only Janet had been married!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I wonder who the father really was. (looking up) She has never told you, Jane, I suppose?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No, Hugo.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: And never will. Nobody was ever so obstinate as Janet.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: JANET always had plenty of will.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Far too much! [pause.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You’ll quite miss Johnny when he goes away from us, Won’t you, Hugo.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. I never thought I could grow so fond of a child. The house will seem empty without him.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I shall miss him too.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: We shall all miss him. (pause, thoughtfully) I wonder if Janet would leave him with us when she goes back to London?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Leave him with us? Altogether, you mean?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m afraid not, Hugo. In fact, I’m quite sure she would not. She’s so fond of Johnny.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I suppose she wouldn’t (pause). I was greatly shocked at what you told me about her the other day, Harriet.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: About her keeping a shop, you mean?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. And going into partnership with a Miss Higgs or Hicks. It all sounds most discreditable.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Deplorable.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She had to do something to keep herself, Hugo.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: No doubt. Still, it can’t be considered a proper sort of position for my daughter. I think she must give it up at once.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: She would only have to take to something else.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Not necessarily. She might come back here to live with us... with Johnny, of course.
Mrs. De. Mullin (astonished)
Live with us?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Why not, Jane?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, of course if you think so, Hugo.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Are you sure you will like to have Janet living at home again, Hugo?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I think it might be the best arrangement. And I shall like to have Johnny here. He’s our only descendant, Harriet, the last of the De Mullins. If you or Jane had had a son it would be different.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Yes.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: As it is I don’t see how we can do anything-better than have them both down here—as Jane doesn’t think Janet would part with Johnny. It would be better for Janet too. It would take her away from her present unsatisfactory surroundings. It would give her a position and independence—everything she now lacks.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I should have thought she was independent now,

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: My dear Jane, how can a woman possibly be independent whose income comes out of selling hats? The only form of independence that is possible or desirable for a woman is that she shall be dependent upon her husband or, if she is unmarried, on her nearest male relative. I am sure you agree with me, Harriet?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Quite, Hugo.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Very well. I will speak to her about it at once.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: I hardly think I would say anything about it to-day, Hugo.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Why not, Jane?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Well, she seems nervous and irritable to-day. I think I should put it off for a day or two.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: My dear Jane, you are always procrastinating. If such an arrangement is to be made the sooner it is made the better. (Goes to window, c., calls) Janet my dear. Janet.
[Pause. Then Janet appears at window, c.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Did you call me, father?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. Come to me for a moment. I want to speak to you. (De Mullin wanders undecidedly to the fireplace. A moment later Janet enters from the garden.) Is Johnny with you?

div.head: JANET
div.p: No. He’s having tea with Ellen. I said he might.
[Pause. Janet comes down.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, your mother and I have been talking over your future.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Have you, father?
[With a quick glance at her mother. Mrs. De Mullin, however, makes no sign.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. We have come to the conclusion that it would be better for you to come back here to live.
[Janet faces round towards her father.

div.head: JANET
div.p: But what would become of the business?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: You will have to give up the business, of course. So much the better. You never ought to have gone into it. It was not at all a suitable occupation for you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: But I like it, father.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Like it! A De Mullin like keeping a shop! Impossible.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Aunt Harriet, I like it. And I’m proud of it.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Nonsense, Janet. Nobody can possibly be proud of keeping a shop.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I am. I made it, you see. It’s my child, like Johnny.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: JANET! Do you understand what you’re doing? I offer you the chance of returning to Brendon to live as my daughter.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I quite understand, father. And I’m much obliged for the offer. Only I decline it. That’s all.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Really!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: The question is, are you to be allowed to decline it, in Johnny’s interests if not your own?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Johnny’s?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Yes. Johnny’s. As long as he was a child it made little difference where he was brought up. Relatively little that is. Now he is getting to an age when early associations are all-important. Living here at Brendon in the home of his ancestors he will grow up worthy of the race from which he is descended. He will be a true De Mullin.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Perhaps I don’t want him to be a true De Mullin, father.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear father, you’re infatuated about your De Mullins. Who are the De Mullins, after all? Mere country squires who lived on here down at Brendon generation after generation. What have they ever done that I should want Johnny to be like them? Nothing. There’s not one of them who has ever distinguished himself in the smallest degree or made his name known outside his native village. The De Mullins are, and have always been, nobodies. Look at their portraits. Is there a single one of them that is worth a second glance? Why they never even had the brains to be painted by a decent artist. With the result that they aren’t worth the canvas they’re painted on. Or is it board? I’d make a bonfire of them if they were mine.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: I would. You seem to think there’s some peculiar virtue about always living in the same place. I believe in people uprooting themselves and doing something with their lives. What was the good of the De Mullins going on living down here century after century, always a little poorer and a little poorer, selling a farm here, mortgaging another there, instead of going out into the world to seek their fortunes? We’ve stayed too long in one place, we De Mullins. We shall never be worth anything sleeping away our lives down at Brendon.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, you are talking foolishly. What you say only makes it clearer to me that you cannot be allowed to live by yourself in London any longer. Such a life is demoralizing to you. You must come back to Brendon.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I shall not come back to Brendon, father. On that I am quite determined.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: My dear, this is not a matter that rests with you. My mind is made up. Hitherto I have only asked you to return. Do not force me to command you.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Command? By what right do you command?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: By the right of a father, Janet. By that right I insist on your obedience.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Obedience! Obedience! I owe no one obedience. I am of full age and can order my life as I please. Is a woman never to be considered old enough to manage her own affairs? Is she to go down to her grave everlastingly under tutelage? Is she always to be obeying a father when she’s not obeying a husband? Well, I, for one, will not submit to such nonsense. I’m sick of this everlasting obedience.

div.head: JANET...!
div.p: [Door opens l. Ellen enters with the lamp. There is a considerable pause, during which Ellen puts down the lamp, turns it up, pulls down the blind and begins to draw the curtains. In the middle of the last process De Mullin intervenes.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: (irritably)
You can leave the curtains, Ellen.

div.head: ELLEN
div.p: Very well, sir.
[Exit Ellen l. with maddening deliberation. Pause.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Father, I’m sorry if what I said vexed you. Perhaps I spoke too strongly.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Very well, Janet. You will remain with us.

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, father, that’s not possible. For Johnny’s sake, as well as my own, it would be madness for us to live down here.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: For Johnny’s sake?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Johnny’s. In London we’re not known, he and I. There he’s simply Johnny Seagrave, the son of a respectable widow who keeps a hat-shop. Here he is the son of Janet De Mullin who ran away from home one night eight years ago and whose name was never mentioned again by her parents until one fine day she turned up with an eight-year-old boy and said she was married. How long would they take to see through that story down here, do you think?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Whose fault is that?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Never mind whose fault it is, Aunt Harriet. The question is, will they see through it or will they not? Of course, they know nothing so far, but I’ve no doubt they suspect. What else have people to do down here but suspect other people? Miss Deanes murmurs her doubts to Mrs. Bulstead and Mrs. Bulstead shakes her head to Miss Deanes. Mrs. Bulstead! What right has she to look down that huge nose of hers at me! She’s had ten children!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: JANET! She’s married.

div.head: JANET
div.p: To Mr. Bulstead! That vulgar animal! You don’t ask me to consider that a merit, do you? No, Mrs. Bulstead shan’t have the chance of sneering at Johnny if I can help it. Or at me either.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet, listen to me. You don’t understand how your father feels about this or how much it means to him. Johnny is his only grandchild—our only descendant. He would adopt him and call him De Mullin, and then the name would not die out. You know how much your father thinks of that and how sorry he has always been that I never had a son.

div.head: JANET
div.p: I know, mother. But when Hester marries...

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: But whom is Hester going to marry? Is she going to marry? I have heard nothing about this. What’s this, Jane? Has something been kept from me?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: No, no, Hugo. Nothing has been kept from you. It’s only some fancy of Janet’s. She thinks Mr. Brown is going to propose to Hester. There’s nothing in it, really.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Mr. Brown! Impossible!

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Quite impossible!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why impossible, father?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: He would never dare to do such a thing. Mr. Brown to have the audacity to propose to my daughter!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Why not, father?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Because he is not of a suitable position. Because the De Mullins cannot be expected to marry people of that class. Because...

div.head: JANET
div.p: I dare say Mr. Brown won’t think of all that. Anyhow, I hope he won’t. I hope he’ll propose to Hester and she’ll accept him and then when they’ve a whole herd of little Browns you can select one of them and make a De Mullin of him, poor little wretch.
[At this moment Hester enters from the garden. An uncomfortable silence falls.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hush, hush, Janet. Here is Hester. Is that you, Hester? Have you come from church?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes, mother.

p.hi: [She comes down, her face looking pale and drawn, and stands by her mother.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You’re very late, dear.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: A little, I stayed on after service was over.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: How very eccentric of you!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I suppose saying one’s prayers does seem eccentric to you, Aunt Harriet?

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: My dear Hester, considering you’d only just finished one service...

div.head: JANET

p.hi: (who has not noticed the look on her sister’s face)

div.p: Well, Aunt Harriet, who was right?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hush, Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear mother, what on earth is there to “hush” about? And what on earth is there to keep Hester in church half an hour after service is over, if it’s not what I told you?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Nothing, dear. Come and give me a kiss.
[Pulling her towards her.
HESTER {repulsing her roughly)
I won’t. Leave me alone, Janet. What has she been saying about me, mother? I insist on knowing.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Nothing, dear. Only some nonsense about you and Mr. Brown. Janet is always talking nonsense.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, Hester. About you and Mr. Brown. Your Mr. Brown. Confess he has asked you to marry him as I said?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Mr. Brown is engaged to be married to Agatha Bulstead. He told me so this evening after service.

div.head: JANET
div.p: He told you!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. He asked me to congratulate him.

div.head: JANET
div.p: The little wretch!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: To Agatha Bulstead? That’s the plain one, isn’t it?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: The third one. Yes.

div.head: JANET
div.p: The plain one! Good heavens, it oughtn’t to be allowed. The children will be little monsters.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: So that’s why you were so long at church?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Yes. I was praying that they might be happy.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Poor Hester!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Are you disappointed, dear?

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I’d rather not talk about it if you don’t mind, mother.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Your father would never have given his consent.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: So Mr. Brown said.

div.head: JANET
div.p: The little worm.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: My dear!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother, isn’t it too contemptible?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I’m bound to say Mr. Brown seems to have behaved in a very fitting manner.

div.head: JANET
div.p: You think so, father?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Certainly. He saw what my objections would be and recognized that they were reasonable. Nothing could be more proper.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, father. I don’t know what you do want. Ten minutes ago you were supposed to be wanting a grandson to adopt. Here’s Hester going the right way to provide one, and you don’t like that either.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: What is all this about, father? What have you all been discussing while I’ve been out?

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: It was nothing about you, Hester.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I’m not sure of that, mother. Anyhow I should like to hear what it was.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Hester, that is not at all a proper tone to use in speaking to your mother.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Please don’t interfere, Aunt Harriet. I suppose I can be trusted to speak to my mother properly by this time.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: You certainly ought to, my dear. You are quite old enough.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Very well then. Perhaps you will be good enough not to dictate to me in future. What was it you were discussing, father?

div.head: JANET
div.p: I’ll tell you, Hester. Father wanted to adopt Johnny. He wanted me to come down here to live altogether.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Indeed? Well, father, understand, please, that if Janet comes down here to live I go!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Hester!

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I will not live in the same house with Janet. Nothing shall induce me. I would rather beg my bread.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That settles it then. Thanks, Hester. I’m glad you had the pluck to say that. You are right. Quite right.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I can do without your approval, Janet.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Of course you can. But you can have it all the same. You never wanted me down here. You always disapproved of my being sent for. I ought never to have come. I wish I hadn’t come. My coming has only done harm to Hester, as she knew it would.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: How harm?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Mr. Brown would have asked Hester to marry him if I hadn’t come. He meant to; I’m sure of it.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: But he said...

div.head: JANET
div.p: I know. But that was only an excuse. Young men aren’t so considerate of their future fathers-inlaw as all that nowadays. No. Mr. Brown heard some story about me from Miss Deanes. Or perhaps the Vicar put him on his guard. Isn’t it so, Hester?
[Hester nods.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: But as your father would never have consented, dear...

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Still, I’d rather he had asked me, mother.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Quite right, Hester! I’m glad you’ve got some wholesome feminine vanity left in your composition. And you’d have said “yes,” like a sensible woman.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Oh, you’re always sneering!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. But I’m going, Hester, going! That’s great thing! Keep your eyes fixed steadily on that and you’ll be able to bear anything else. That reminds me. (Goes to door, l., and calls loudly into the hall.) Johnny! Johnny!

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Really, Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh, I forgot. It’s not genteel to call into the passage, is it? I ought to have rung. I apologise, Aunt Harriet. (Calls again) Johnny!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Why are you calling Johnny?

div.head: JANET
div.p: To tell him to put on his hat and coat, mother dear. I’m going to the station.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: You’re going to-night?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, father, to-night. I’ve done harm enough down here. I’m going away.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Do you want me, Mummie?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes. Run and put on your things and say goodbye to Cook and Ellen and tell Robert to put in the pony. Mother’s going back to London.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: Are we going now, Mummie?

div.head: JANET
div.p: As fast as the train can carry us. And tell Ellen to lock my trunk for me and give you the key. Run along.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Lock your trunk! But you’ve not packed?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh yes, I have. Everything’s packed, down to my last shoelace. I don’t know how often I haven’t packed and unpacked during the last five days.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: You meant to leave us then, Janet? You’ve been wanting to leave us all the time?

div.head: JANET
div.p: Yes, mother. I’ve been wanting to leave you. I can’t stay here any longer. Brendon stifles me. It has too many ghosts. I suppose it’s your ridiculous De Mullins.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: I know, father. That’s blasphemy, isn’t it? But I can’t help it. I must go. I’ve been meaning to tell you every day for the last four days, but somehow I always put it off.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Understand me, Janet. If you leave this house to-night you leave it for ever.

div.head: JANET
div.p: All right, father.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Understand, too, that if you leave it you are never to hold any communication either with me or with any one in it henceforward. You are cut off from the family. I will never see you or recognize you in any way, or speak to you again as long as I live.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear father, why are you so angry? Is there anything so dreadful in my wanting to live in London instead of in the country?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Why am I angry! Why am I...!

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Sh! Hugo! You mustn’t excite yourself. You know the doctor said...

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Be quiet, Jane! (turning furiously to Janet) Why am I angry! You disgrace the family. You have a child, that poor fatherless boy....

div.head: JANET
div.p: Oh come, I could have got along quite well without a father if it comes to that. And so could Hester.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother, what has father ever done for Hester or me except try and prevent us from doing something we wanted to do? Hester wanted to marry Mr. Brown. Father wouldn’t have allowed her. He’s not genteel enough to marry a De Mullin. I want to go back to my shop. Father objects to that. That’s not genteel enough for a De Mullin either. Well, hang all the De Mullins, say I.

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: I forbid you to speak of your family in that way-of my family! I forbid it! It is an outrage. Your ancestors were honourable men and pure women. They did their duty in the position in which they were born, and handed on their name untarnished to their children. Hitherto our honour has been unsullied. You have sullied it. You have brought shame upon your parents and shame upon your son, and that shame you can never wipe out. If you had in you a spark of human feeling, if you were not worthless and heartless you would blush to look me in the face or your child in the face. But you are utterly hardened. I ought never to have offered to receive you back into this house. I ought never to have consented to see you again. I was wrong. I regret it. You are unfit for the society of decent people. Go back to London. Take up the wretched trade you practise there. It is what you are fit for.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That’s exactly what I think, father. As we agree about it why make such a fuss?

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet....

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Father, don’t argue with her. It’s no use. (solemnly) Leave her to God.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Hester, Hester, don’t deceive yourself. In your heart you envy me my baby, and you know it.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: I do not.

div.head: JANET
div.p: You do. Time is running on with you, my dear. You’re twenty-eight. Just the age that I was when I met my lover. Yes, my lover. In a few years you will be too old for love, too old to have children. So soon it passeth away and we are gone. Your best years are slipping by and you are growing faded and cross and peevish. Already the lines are hardening about your mouth and the hollows coming under your eyes. You will be an old woman before your time unless you marry and have children. And what will you do then? Keep a lap-dog, I suppose, or sit up at night with a sick cockatoo like Miss Deanes. Miss Deanes! Even she has a heart somewhere about her. Do you imagine she wouldn’t rather give it to her babies than snivel over poultry? No, Hester, make good use of your youth, my dear. It won’t last always. And once gone it is gone for ever. (Hester bursts into tears.) There, there, Hester! I’m sorry. I oughtn’t to have spoken like that. It wasn’t kind. Forgive me. (Hester weep more and more violently.) Hester, don’t cry like that. I can’t bear to hear you. I was angry and said more than I should. I didn’t mean to vex you. Come, dear, you mustn’t give way like that or you’ll make yourself ill. Dry your eyes and let me see you smile. (Caressing her. Hester, who has begun by resisting her feebly, gradually allows herself to be soothed.) That’s better! My dear, what a sight you’ve made of yourself! But all women are hideous when they’ve been crying. It makes their noses red and that’s dreadfully unbecoming. (Hester sobs out a laugh). No. You mustn’t begin to cry again or I shall scold you. I shall, really.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: You seem to think every woman ought to behave as shamefully as you did.

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, Hester. I don’t think that. To do as I did needs pluck and brains—and five hundred pounds. Everything most women haven’t got, poor things. So they must marry or remain childless. You must marry—the next curate. I suppose the Bulsteads will buy Mr. Brown a living as he’s marrying the plainest of the daughters. It’s the least they can do. But that’s no reason why I should marry unless I choose.

div.head: MRS. CLOUSTON
div.p: Well, I’ve never heard of anything so disgraceful. I thought Janet at least had the grace to be ashamed of what she did!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Ashamed? Ashamed of wanting to have a child? What on earth were women created for, Aunt Harriet, if not to have children?
MRS. CLOUSTON To marry and have children.

div.head: JANET
div.p: My dear Aunt Harriet, women had children thousands of years before marriage was invented. I dare say they will go on doing so thousands of years after it has ceased to exist.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: Well, mother, that’s how I feel. And I believe it’s how all wholesome women feel if they would only acknowledge it. I wanted to have a child. I always did from the time when I got too old to play with dolls. Not an adopted child or a child of some one else’s, but a baby of my very own. Of course I wanted to marry. That’s the ordinary way a woman wants to be a mother nowadays, I suppose. But time went on and nobody came forward, and I saw myself getting old and my chance slipping away. Then I met-never mind. And I fell in love with him. Or perhaps I only fell in love with love. I don’t know. It was so splendid to find some one at last who really cared for me as women should be cared for! Not to talk to because I was clever or to play tennis with because I was strong, but to kiss me and to make love to me! Yes! To make love to me!

div.head: DE MULLIN
div.p: Listen to me, my girl. You say that now, and I dare say you believe it. But when you are older, when Johnny is grown up, you will bitterly repent having brought into the world a child who can call no man father.

div.head: JANET
div.p: Never! Never! That I’m sure of. Whatever happens, even if Johnny should come to hate me for what I did, I shall always be glad to have been his mother. At least I shall have lived. These poor women who go through life listless and dull, who have never felt the joys and the pains a mother feels, how they would envy me if they knew! If they knew! To know that a child is your very own, is a part of you. That you have faced sickness and pain and death itself for it. That it is yours and nothing can take it from you because no one can understand its wants as you do. To feel it’s soft breath on your cheek, to soothe it when it is fretful and still it when it cries, that is motherhood and that is glorious!
[Johnny runs in by the door on the left. He is obviously in the highest spirits at the thought of going home.

div.head: JOHNNY
div.p: The trap is round, Mummie, and the luggage is in.

div.head: JANET
div.p: That’s right. Good-bye, father. (He does not move) Say good-bye to your grandfather, Johnny. You won’t see him again.
[De Mullin kisses Johnny.

div.head: MRS. DE MULLIN
div.p: Janet!

div.head: JANET
div.p: No, mother. It’s best not. (Kisses her) It would only be painful for father. Good-bye, Aunt Harriet. Good-bye, Hester.
[Looks at Hester doubtfully. Hester rises, goes to her slowly and kisses her.

div.head: HESTER
div.p: Good-bye. .
[Exeunt Johnny and Janet by the door the right.

div.head: DE MULLIN

p.hi: (his grey head bowed on his chest as Mrs De Mullin timidly lays her hand on his shoulder)

div.p: The last of the De Mullins! The last of the De Mullins!
